APP: solitaire-atelier
CURRENT PHASE: design_discussion
PHASE PURPOSE: Decide UX flows, information architecture, key screens/states, and the design principles that govern them.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

## Final Output

This is a single-app decision, not a portfolio parent. The prompt asks for exactly one thing — a native iOS Klondike solitaire game — with Game/Stats/Settings implemented as tabs *within* that one app, not as separate sibling projects. No portfolio-json manifest is emitted.

**Selected app:**
- Category: Games/Card
- Slug: `solitaire-atelier` (matches the existing working directory)
- Promise: a real, fully-correct Klondike solitaire game with a bespoke tactile card system, local-only stats/settings, undo, and win detection — visually distinctive enough to be screenshot-worthy
- Target user: casual players who want a fast, trustworthy five-minute session, plus a design-literate audience who will judge it against a premium visual bar
- Build flag: `true`

**Rejected alternatives:** splitting Stats, Settings, or a card-back/theme pack into separate sibling apps — explicitly rejected as scope-inflation that contradicts the locked non-goals (no bundle sprawl, no multi-variant solitaire) and would fragment the single-session experience the prompt is actually asking for.

**Rationale:** No second category or variant is implied anywhere in the prompt; inventing sibling projects here would add state-sync complexity, dilute the one signature visual/interaction hook into disconnected shells, and violate decisions already locked in `prompt_contract` (DEC-prompt_contract-010, non-goals). One caveat flagged for downstream phases: this phase being "obvious" doesn't mean the hard part is solved — the actual product risk is whether the design/build phases deliver a card glyph system that clears legibility at true device size, per [REDACTED:high_entropy].

## Final Output

**Growth mechanism, now settled:** No challenge-seed/replay feature. It's explicitly rejected because it would require a second, hand-rolled deterministic RNG living alongside the real shuffle path (since Swift's system RNG isn't a documented, cross-OS-version-reproducible algorithm), which threatens the locked "fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game" guarantee and spends correctness-tier engineering effort on an unproven behavioral bet. Instead, v1 gets a one-tap native share sheet on the win screen that shares a rendered image of the completed board (foundations, with a "solved in 4:32"-style caption baked in). This is pure presentation — render an image, hand it to the system share sheet — with zero backend, zero new RNG path, and zero in-app mechanism for a recipient to do anything but look at a picture, so it doesn't brush against the locked no-social/no-multiplayer non-goal. Growth otherwise remains organic screenshot/word-of-mouth discovery, now with slightly less friction at the one moment a player is most likely to want to share.

## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

VOTE_DECISION: YES

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 2**

Round 2 closed most of the gap. Codex came back and explicitly sided with Claude's read on tap-to-move — auto-routing was the wrong call because destination choice in Klondike is genuinely strategic, not cosmetic. They landed on a clean synthesis together: tap a card, and if it only has one legal home, it just goes there immediately (fast, feels instant, covers the common case); if it has more than one legal home, all of them light up and you tap the one you want; if it has none, nothing lights up and you get the same "blocked" feedback as any illegal move — which doubles as free, honest status feedback. ### Round 2


**Codex (Design Lead · Skeptic) — Round 2**

Claude, I’m with you on this fork: for this phase we shouldn’t pretend “slice 1” is the final app, because nothing in this phase explicitly guarantees a guaranteed follow-on increment. The earlier slice framing was valid engineering sequencing, not a product scope contract. In app_features, we’re defining the thing that gets built and judged. If we leave out real Settings and real Stats now, we inherit the very “placeholder-surface” risk DEC-prompt_contract-011 was trying to ban, regardless of how clean the game core is. I know you called out smaller finished app, and I think that cuts the other way here — finished means no missing required surfaces the user explicitly asked for, not “engine-complete minus two tabs.”

Codex, your concern about correctness risk from expanding scope is still valid, but there’s a cheaper way to keep that discipline without deferring UI asks. We can make Settings + Stats real with default-safe values and no fabricated UI from day one, while reusing the already-logged silent game events. Stats can open with honest initial state (0/0/N/A), a live-updating streak, and per-mode splits backed by logged sessions once implemented in full from round 3 onwards. Settings can be fully real with three controls and non-negotiable semantics: draw toggle gated behind new game, card back live-update, timer toggle wired to timer start/pause logic, plus local-only disclaimer copy. That’s work, but it doesn’t destabilize the move engine.

On draw-3, I agree with you both that it’s a bigger behavioral surface than just a UI toggle, and [REDACTED:high_entropy] already made draw-3 detection rules explicit for only draw-1. That means in this phase if draw-3 is in-scope, we must own the correct stuck-detection behavior for it now or explicitly split its behavior into a separate feature line with a real algorithm. I don’t want a silent “setting that doesn’t mean what it says” failure. If we keep draw-3 as in-scope, the acceptance criteria should include a concrete rule: draw behavior, legal moves, and no-move detection are computed correctly under draw-3 with unlimited redeal, not via draw-1 shortcut.

So my vote for this round is: promote Settings/Stats from “could” to must in this phase, keep them in the same TabView shell as real peers, and keep draw-3 in scope as a core requirement only if the build plan can own a correct implementation path; if not, we must explicitly lock a named follow-on increment before closing this phase. I’d rather fail early on scope honesty than ship an app whose user-facing promises are split between visible and deferred features.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Pragmatist) — Round 2**

Codex, I actually think we're closer than the coordinator's "CONSENSUS: NO" makes it look, because look at what you actually put in the requirements-json you both apparently fed the coordinator — R-019 through R-021 mark Stats, Settings, and draw-3 as `"core": true`. That's not a compromise position, that's the coordinator siding with my read of the situation while formally calling it unresolved. So let me just say directly what I think everyone's dancing around: nobody in this entire pipeline has named a phase where "slice 2" gets built. app_features feeds into design and build phases for one app. If we ship your MoSCoW as written — Settings/Stats/draw-3 sitting in "Could," gated behind "once slice-1 build is stable" — there is no mechanism in this factory that comes back later and builds them. That's not sequencing risk, that's just cutting three things the original prompt names by name and that DEC-prompt_contract-011 explicitly locks as automatic-reject if missing. I'd rather we argue about this now, loudly, than find out at the adherence gate that "could-have" quietly became "never-have."

That said, I want to take the "build size" constraint in the phase rules seriously instead of just steamrolling past it, because pretending this is free would be its own kind of dishonesty. Here's my actual case for why the full triad still fits: the hard, risky, novel engineering in this whole app was never Settings or Stats — it's the rules engine, run-relocation move logic, persistence integrity, and the bespoke card art passing the legibility gate. A Settings screen with three toggles and a Stats screen with four numbers per draw mode is comparatively cheap once the underlying data model exists — and it already does, because DEC-next_steps_small-007 had us building the event-recording schema from day one specifically so it'd be ready for this. Codex, you wrote should-have item "local stats/settings persistence architecture prepared for future settings/stats screens" — I'd argue that's most of the actual engineering cost already accounted for on your own list, just pointed at a phase-2 that doesn't exist. So my counter-proposal on where to actually cut for build-size reasons: gut the should/could tier harder, not the must tier. Win-screen share sheet, live drag (single or multi-card), extra card-back variants beyond two, ambient parallax/shadow micro-polish — all of that goes, cleanly, no argument, because none of it is named in the original prompt as a concrete requirement the way Stats and Settings are.

On draw-3, I want to actually solve the thing the coordinator flagged instead of leaving it as an open risk again, because "ship it as core but nobody designed the stuck-detection" is exactly the kind of gap that turns into a shipped bug. [REDACTED:high_entropy] was right to say the draw-1 static-pass shortcut doesn't transfer, and here's concretely why: in draw-1, every card sitting in stock or waste is guaranteed to eventually surface as the waste top on its own, one at a time, so "treat every stock+waste card as a hypothetical waste-top" is exact. In draw-3, cards surface in groups of three and only the front of each group is playable until you draw past it, and which cards end up grouped together shifts every time the pile reshuffles back from waste to stock — so proving exact reachability is a real combinatorial problem I don't think we should try to solve precisely under this build's time budget. My pragmatic fix: reuse the same permissive static pass for draw-3 too — treat every card currently in stock or waste as a hypothetical candidate, exactly like draw-1 — but document explicitly that this is a conservative approximation, not an exact proof, and design it to fail toward "don't declare stuck" rather than "falsely declare stuck." That's the right direction to be wrong in: a board that's actually stuck but doesn't show the stuck modal yet is mildly annoying, the player just keeps drawing and finds out; a board that falsely tells the player "you're stuck, game over" when a real move existed is a much worse trust violation, on an app whose entire pitch is "we don't lie to you about your own data." I'd rather ship a slightly conservative stuck-check than an exact one we don't have time to prove correct.

Last thing, since I promised concrete acceptance criteria and mostly gestured at the idea last round instead of writing them: the Stats screen needs an explicit empty state before any game exists for that mode, and that's not optional polish — it's the global "every screen needs empty/loading/success/error" rule colliding directly with the "N/A best time" and "no fabricated data" rules we've already locked. Acceptance criteria should read something like: on first launch, before any game is completed in a given draw mode, that mode's stats show a real empty state ("0 games played" or equivalent), never a placeholder number, never the other mode's numbers, and never blank. And for the draw-mode setting specifically: selecting draw-3 while a draw-1 game is mid-progress must trigger the same confirmation pattern already locked for New Game — if the player confirms, the current game is discarded and a fresh draw-3 deal starts; if they cancel, the setting value doesn't change and the in-progress game is untouched. That's the kind of criterion that's actually testable by someone poking at the app, not just prose we hope gets implemented faithfully.

Draw-3 stuck-detection got a real answer too. Claude walked through why the draw-1 static-pass shortcut can't just be copy-pasted (draw-3 surfaces cards in shifting groups of three, so exact reachability is a genuine combinatorial problem this build shouldn't try to solve precisely) and proposed reusing the same permissive treat-every-stock/waste-card-as-reachable approach for draw-3, but biased deliberately toward under-declaring stuck rather than over-declaring it — a false "not stuck yet" just means the player keeps drawing, but a false "you're stuck, game over" is a real trust violation on an app whose whole pitch is honesty about the player's own data. Codex didn't get a chance to respond to this specific mechanism, but it's a direct, load-bearing answer to the exact gap Codex raised in round 1 (own draw-3's detection or name a follow-on phase) — and since Codex already conceded draw-3 must be "core" this round, I'm treating this as the natural resolution rather than a leftover fork.

Claude also nailed down concrete, testable acceptance criteria for the two fuzziest must-haves: Stats needs a real per-mode empty state on first launch (never a placeholder number, never borrowing the other mode's data, never blank), and switching draw mode mid-game routes through the same confirmation pattern already locked for New Game (confirm discards and re-deals in the new mode; cancel leaves both the setting and the in-progress game untouched).

## Final Output

The full triad — Game, Stats, and Settings — ships as real, non-placeholder screens in this build, in one TabView shell with resume-first launch into the active game. Draw-1 and draw-3 are both real, fully-working modes: draw-3 gets its own stuck-detection approach (the same permissive stock+waste-as-reachable static pass as draw-1, explicitly documented as a conservative approximation that's biased to under-declare "stuck" rather than falsely tell a player the game is over when a move still exists), and switching between draw modes mid-game requires the same New-Game-style confirmation before it takes effect. Stats tracks games played/won, best time, and streak separately per draw mode, with a real empty state before any game completes in that mode and "N/A" for best time whenever the timer is off — never a fabricated number. Settings carries all three named controls (draw mode gated behind confirmation, card-back live-swappable, timer on/off) plus the local-only data disclosure line. Everything from the earlier slice-1 correctness discipline stays intact underneath this: the shared tap-to-move/run-relocation validation core, atomic no-encryption logical-state persistence, full undo, explicit win/stuck terminal states, silent event logging, deal/flip gated to fresh deals only, portrait lock, and the full non-goals list (no live drag, no share sheet, no multiplayer/IAP/accounts/cloud sync) — all held as-is. The scope room needed to afford Stats/Settings/draw-3 comes out of the should/could tier instead: win-screen sharing, live interactive drag, and extra card-back variants beyond the minimum are the things actually cut, not the screens the original prompt named by name.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

I would reject the default stock iOS solitaire look on three concrete points: first, replace plain rounded-rect cards with custom bespoke faces, backs, and paper grain from one generative grammar; second, swap the flat gray/blue grid into a textured felt+laminated table field with semantic depth layers so every pile has visual affordance before interaction; third, replace generic UIKit card rows with custom hit-target aware stack views that can express destination highlights without turning a face-down pile into a random icon grid, and avoid default chrome like plain lists and system forms in all key screens.

Screen inventory for this phase is fixed at three peers in TabView: Game, Stats, Settings, with the app launching directly to Game and restoring saved state if present.  
The Game screen has an active layout state: active in-progress game (deal/flip already done), selecting source card state (candidate run computed), destination-choice highlight state for multi-destination taps, blocked-move feedback state, win terminal, and stuck-terminal.  
The same screen also has small utility states that are visible and recoverable: empty-save recovery when decode fails, invalid-saved-state error with reset fallback, and pending confirmation state for New Game or in-progress draw-mode switch; no hidden transitions, no silent resets.  
Stats has three explicit states per mode: never-played empty state per draw mode with explanatory icon+copy+action, populated success state with games won/played/best time/streak, and local persistence error state if the stats file cannot be parsed (with reset/rebuild option, never fake numbers).  
Settings has live states for Card Back selection, Draw mode, and Timer toggle with immediate, local persistence confirmation, plus disclosure-copy state about device-local persistence and an explicit “restart required” confirmation path for draw-mode changes while a game is in progress.  

Primary user flow starts in Game: launch resolves active state, user sees tableau immediately, taps a source card, app highlights legal destinations or runs auto-accept with haptics and spring motion, or indicates blocked move if none. Every legal move is one tap-to-move flow; run moves happen as a whole run unit while live drag remains out of scope. Stock draw updates table state and timer if it has not started. Undo is always available in-game as an inline action and returns exact state. On terminal condition (win or stuck) the game shows a full-state action sheet with New Game and return-to-game context; New Game always asks if current game is unfinished. Stats and Settings are always reachable via tabs, and Settings draw-mode change while active game follows the same confirmation component as New Game.

State model should be explicit and deterministic: for Game, persisted logical state is {deck pools, face-up flags, active draw mode, timer status/start offset, move history pointer, terminal flags}. For Stats, state is {per-mode totals: games played, won, best time optional, streak, N/A marker}. For Settings, state is {draw mode, card back id, timer enabled, disclosure acknowledged}; all changes are local and immediate except draw-mode, which is confirmation-gated. In the UI layer, each of these has success, loading, and error surfaces even though there is no backend; loading is relevant during startup restoration and settings persistence writes, error only appears for decode/persistence recovery.

Accessibility is not optional on this custom-card stack, so every card must expose explicit labels (“Seven of Hearts, tableau column three, face up” style), directional order in VoiceOver, and non-color-only suit/sequence cues. Motion must respect reduced-motion by using gentler fade/translate in place of full spring/deal arcs where needed, and legal/illegal move feedback should be perceivable through haptics plus non-visual state.  

The smallest risky but highest-value cut is this: keep draw-1 and draw-3, two draw modes in one coherent engine, plus immediate TabView triad (Game/Stats/Settings), but hold off adding alternate interaction surfaces that dilute the rules pipeline; everything else should be built as part of correctness and state honesty first. The biggest objection I would raise against this direction is visual ambition can still outrun card-legibility at true on-device width, so the design spec must preserve a hard legibility gate as a release gate, not a design review note, and the final build must keep the 45–50pt card width playable and unambiguous.

## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

VOTE_DECISION: YES

- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] Correctness, rules-fidelity, and deterministic local state always outrank visual polish whenever they compete for build/complexity budget, and any such trade-off must be logged rather than silently resolved.
  rationale: The original prompt itself states visual ambition must not cost playability/correctness; this fleet has a documented history of visual ambition winning while correctness quietly breaks.
  rejected: Letting a later phase silently ship the prettier but rules-broken version
  constraints: Every later phase must justify any cut to gameplay/state logic; cuts come out of the art system first
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] The 52-card face system (+ back) must be a systematic/generative/parametric design — shared type and icon components plus programmatic layout rules — not 52 independently hand-illustrated cards.
  rationale: Hand-illustrating 52 unique faces to a consistent standard is a scope trap likely to yield a few great cards and many generic ones, which itself fails the prompt's own 'looks like a stock tutorial' test.
  rejected: 52 independently hand-illustrated card faces
  constraints: Face system must be visually consistent across the full deck and card back in one shared visual grammar
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] All persistence is strictly single-device local storage (UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData) with no CloudKit container; no iCloud or cross-device sync of saved game, stats, or settings.
  rationale: Zero-network/zero-account constraint is interpreted to forbid any sync mechanism even though CloudKit-synced data would still technically be 'local' per device — closes a loophole someone could exploit later thinking it's harmless.
  rejected: Allowing CloudKit sync of save/stats/settings since the data itself originates locally
  constraints: No CloudKit container, no NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, no networking APIs anywhere in the codebase
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] Stats and best-time are tracked separately for draw-1 vs draw-3, never combined.
  rationale: Draw-1 and draw-3 have materially different win rates and completion times; a combined metric would misrepresent the player's actual performance.
  rejected: Single combined stats/best-time pool across both draw modes
  constraints: Stats screen must present or select per-mode figures, not an averaged/merged number
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] When the timer is off, best time displays as 'N/A', never a fabricated 0:00 or a stale prior value.
  rationale: Fleet-wide rule against claiming outcomes/state that didn't truly happen; showing a fake time would be lying about data that was never captured.
  rejected: Showing 0:00 or the last recorded time when timer is disabled
  constraints: Stats screen must branch explicitly on timer-enabled state per session
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Card back selection can change live at any time; changing draw mode (1 vs 3) requires starting a new game.
  rationale: Card back is purely cosmetic and safe to swap mid-game; draw mode changes the legal deal/hand semantics, so applying it mid-game would corrupt in-progress state.
  rejected: Allowing draw-mode changes to apply instantly mid-game
  constraints: Settings screen must gate draw-mode changes behind a new-game action or confirmation
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] Klondike is locked as single-deck, 7 tableau columns, 4 foundations (one per suit), ascending same-suit foundation moves, alternating-color descending tableau sequences, and King-only placement into empty tableau columns.
  rationale: Removes ambiguity in the prompt so later phases build against one unambiguous rule set instead of rediscovering rules mid-implementation.
  rejected: Leaving rule variants (e.g., multi-deck, unrestricted empty-column placement) open for later interpretation
  constraints: All move-validation logic must conform to this exact rule set

**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 3**

Codex, I think you’re right that we shouldn’t pour complexity into this slice, and I agree with keeping drag to a later increment. But I have to push back harder on one detail you just brushed: if we keep tap-to-move to “single card only,” we’re not just simplifying UX, we’re changing the rule semantics we already locked as Klondike in DEC-prompt_contract-007. In canonical Klondike, a playable move is a legal face-up descending alternating sequence, not just a single card. Even if many game states remain solvable without it, this app is promising “correct Klondike,” and that promise is what gives this branch credibility.

Claude’s catch in round 2 is the one that matters most now: interpreting DEC-next_steps_small-002 as “no live run-drag” does not force us to ban valid run relocation as a game rule. We can (and should) support run moves through the tap-to-move path, with zero live drag state. Concretely: when a source is selected, compute the maximal face-up alternating-descending sequence starting at that card, validate the sequence destination via the same shared `attemptMove` path, and animate the whole block moving when confirmed. This also preserves the “single destination auto-exec” fast path and the multi-destination confirm path we already locked, and it gives us rule-complete semantics without importing the fragile continuous gesture pipeline yet.

So I’d lock this as: tap interaction supports moving a valid sequence as the unit, while live multi-card drag remains deferred. That keeps this slice clean and avoids a legal-move false-negative gap later when the user actually starts testing strategy depth.

On the persistence side, I think we should kill the encryption-if-possible phrasing entirely. There’s no PII, no credentials, no secrets here; adding an encryption layer is not just unnecessary, it adds migration and failure-mode risk (device-locked states, keychain surprises, platform edge behavior) with no user-facing gain for this brief. Keep it plain local FileManager/SwiftData/Defaults with atomic write/temp-swap as already decided in [REDACTED:high_entropy].

Orientation: I’d keep `portrait-only` at the app level, but not force iPhone-only unless someone adds it as an explicit schedule decision. The constraints already say portrait-first; iPad-in-portrait is fine and keeps the product from appearing intentionally capped. If we later see layout debt there, we can scope it, but we shouldn’t over-constrain now.

Timer semantics should stay exactly as [REDACTED:high_entropy] says: start on first state-mutating action (`confirmed move` or `stock draw`) and never on selection/tap-highlight or deal animation. A user who is just browsing or inspecting shouldn’t have their run clock ticking.

One more hard point to pin before we lose steam: we’ve got most of the right UX and lifecycle posture now (fresh-deal-only animation, static draw-1 stuck pass, themed LaunchScreen, New Game confirmation, non-placeholder start path). I’d like these to be treated as locked now so round 3 doesn’t leak back into them.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 3**

Codex, you came back and fully validated the tap-mechanics synthesis, and I think that's the right call — but I want to push the run-move issue harder this round since you haven't weighed in on it yet and the coordinator flagged it as the thing we actually need to close. Let me make it concrete instead of abstract: imagine a tableau column with a red 6 face-up, and stacked on top of it (added later, validly) a black 5. Somewhere else on the board there's an exposed black 7. In real Klondike, I tap the 6, both the 6 and 5 lift together as a unit, and they land on the 7 — because the 6-5 pairing is a legal alternating-descending sequence and moving it preserves that structure at the new location. Now here's the part that actually matters for correctness: there is no way to reconstruct this outcome with single-card-only moves unless the 5 happens to have some other legal home somewhere on the board right now — move 5 away, move 6 onto the 7, move 5 back onto 6. Often it won't have one; that's frequently the exact reason the run needs to move together in the first place. If our move model can't execute this, a board where that 6-5-onto-7 relocation was the only way forward isn't just harder to play, it's unwinnable under our own rules engine even though it's a completely standard, legal Klondike position. And because [REDACTED:high_entropy] just locked a stuck-detection algorithm that checks "does any legal move exist," a board like that would get correctly flagged as stuck by our own logic, when a real Klondike player would look at the same board and immediately see the run-move that gets them unstuck. We'd be shipping false stuck-detections that are actually true-within-our-broken-move-model but false against the real game. That's about as bad a correctness bug as this app can have, since it's exactly the failure mode everyone from per_app_product_brief onward has said is worse than any ad-laden competitor.

The fix doesn't cost what I think DEC-next_steps_small-002 was actually worried about. That decision was written to kill live interactive drag — continuous finger tracking, recomputing drop targets frame-by-frame, mid-gesture z-order fights between adjacent columns. None of that shows up here. Tapping any face-up tableau card can just select "that card plus every face-up card stacked after it toward the exposed end" as one atomic unit — and I'd point out this is always well-defined, because every face-up card that got placed on top of another face-up card only got there through a validated move that required it to be one rank lower and opposite color. So the run structure is guaranteed consistent by construction; there's no ambiguity to resolve at selection time, just "walk from the tapped card to the end of the pile." Compute the headmost card's rank/suit, find legal destinations for it exactly like we already do for a single card, highlight, confirm, animate the whole group moving together. Same shared `attemptMove` core, same tap-select-confirm flow we already agreed on, just operating on a card-group instead of a single card. I want this locked explicitly this round: tap-to-move includes relocating a validly-stacked tableau run as a unit, and "multi-card run-drag deferred" refers specifically to the live drag gesture, not to this rules capability.

On the smaller loose ends — I'm conceding one and holding one. I'm conceding the timer question to your version: first state-mutating action, not bare tap-select. Thinking about it more, a tap-select in the multi-destination case is genuinely exploratory — a careful player checking what a card's options are before committing shouldn't have the clock start on them for looking, and given our own synthesis this round already means a single-destination tap resolves instantly into a mutation anyway, there's no real case where "select" and "mutate" diverge except the one where letting the clock wait makes more sense. You're right, I was overreaching in round 1. On device scope, I'll drop the iPhone-only push too — "portrait-only across whatever's supported" gets the actual risk I cared about (no half-baked landscape layout) without me inventing a device-support decision nobody asked for; if iPad support is a real question it should get its own decision later with an actual reason attached, not get smuggled in as a side effect of an orientation lock. But I do want the encryption question fully closed, not left as your original "not a dependency" softness — say it outright: no encryption layer, plain FileManager/UserDefaults/SwiftData, because there's genuinely nothing in this app's data that needs it and every encrypted-storage path is a new failure surface (Keychain access timing on a locked device, key migration) for a threat that doesn't exist here. I'd rather this phase say that plainly than leave a door open that a build phase might walk through "just to be safe."

**Codex (Design Lead · Skeptic) — Round 2**

Claude, I’m with you on this fork: for this phase we shouldn’t pretend “slice 1” is the final app, because nothing in this phase explicitly guarantees a guaranteed follow-on increment. The earlier slice framing was valid engineering sequencing, not a product scope contract. In app_features, we’re defining the thing that gets built and judged. If we leave out real Settings and real Stats now, we inherit the very “placeholder-surface” risk DEC-prompt_contract-011 was trying to ban, regardless of how clean the game core is. I know you called out smaller finished app, and I think that cuts the other way here — finished means no missing required surfaces the user explicitly asked for, not “engine-complete minus two tabs.”

Codex, your concern about correctness risk from expanding scope is still valid, but there’s a cheaper way to keep that discipline without deferring UI asks. We can make Settings + Stats real with default-safe values and no fabricated UI from day one, while reusing the already-logged silent game events. Stats can open with honest initial state (0/0/N/A), a live-updating streak, and per-mode splits backed by logged sessions once implemented in full from round 3 onwards. Settings can be fully real with three controls and non-negotiable semantics: draw toggle gated behind new game, card back live-update, timer toggle wired to timer start/pause logic, plus local-only disclaimer copy. That’s work, but it doesn’t destabilize the move engine.

On draw-3, I agree with you both that it’s a bigger behavioral surface than just a UI toggle, and [REDACTED:high_entropy] already made draw-3 detection rules explicit for only draw-1. That means in this phase if draw-3 is in-scope, we must own the correct stuck-detection behavior for it now or explicitly split its behavior into a separate feature line with a real algorithm. I don’t want a silent “setting that doesn’t mean what it says” failure. If we keep draw-3 as in-scope, the acceptance criteria should include a concrete rule: draw behavior, legal moves, and no-move detection are computed correctly under draw-3 with unlimited redeal, not via draw-1 shortcut.

So my vote for this round is: promote Settings/Stats from “could” to must in this phase, keep them in the same TabView shell as real peers, and keep draw-3 in scope as a core requirement only if the build plan can own a correct implementation path; if not, we must explicitly lock a named follow-on increment before closing this phase. I’d rather fail early on scope honesty than ship an app whose user-facing promises are split between visible and deferred features.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Pragmatist) — Round 2**

Codex, I actually think we're closer than the coordinator's "CONSENSUS: NO" makes it look, because look at what you actually put in the requirements-json you both apparently fed the coordinator — R-019 through R-021 mark Stats, Settings, and draw-3 as `"core": true`. That's not sequencing risk, that's just cutting three things the original prompt names by name and that DEC-prompt_contract-011 explicitly locks as automatic-reject if missing. I'd rather we argue about this now, loudly, than find out at the adherence gate that "could-have" quietly became "never-have."

That said, I want to take the "build size" constraint in the phase rules seriously instead of just steamrolling past it, because pretending this is free would be its own kind of dishonesty. Here's my actual case for why the full triad still fits: the hard, risky, novel engineering in this whole app was never Settings or Stats — it's the rules engine, run-relocation move logic, persistence integrity, and the bespoke card art passing the legibility gate. A Settings screen with three toggles and a Stats screen with four numbers per draw mode is comparatively cheap once the underlying data model exists — and it already does, because DEC-next_steps_small-007 had us building the event-recording schema from day one specifically so it'd be ready for this. Codex, you wrote should-have item "local stats/settings persistence architecture prepared for future settings/stats screens" — I'd argue that's most of the actual engineering cost already accounted for on your own list, just pointed at a phase-2 that doesn't exist. So my counter-proposal on where to actually cut for build-size reasons: gut the should/could tier harder, not the must tier. Win-screen share sheet, live drag (single or multi-card), extra card-back variants beyond two, ambient parallax/shadow micro-polish — all of that goes, cleanly, no argument, because none of it is named in the original prompt as a concrete requirement the way Stats and Settings are.

On draw-3, I want to actually solve the thing the coordinator flagged instead of leaving it as an open risk again, because "ship it as core but nobody designed the stuck-detection" is exactly the kind of gap that turns into a shipped bug. [REDACTED:high_entropy] was right to say the draw-1 static-pass shortcut doesn't transfer, and here's concretely why: in draw-1, every card sitting in stock or waste is guaranteed to eventually surface as the waste top on its own, one at a time, so "treat every stock+waste card as a hypothetical waste-top" is exact. In draw-3, cards surface in groups of three and only the front of each group is playable until you draw past it, and which cards end up grouped together shifts every time the pile reshuffles back from waste to stock — so proving exact reachability is a real combinatorial problem I don't think we should try to solve precisely under this build's time budget. My pragmatic fix: reuse the same permissive static pass for draw-3 too — treat every card currently in stock or waste as a hypothetical candidate, exactly like draw-1 — but document explicitly that this is a conservative approximation, not an exact proof, and design it to fail toward "don't declare stuck" rather than "falsely declare stuck." That's the right direction to be wrong in: a board that's actually stuck but doesn't show the stuck modal yet is mildly annoying, the player just keeps drawing and finds out; a board that falsely tells the player "you're stuck, game over" when a real move existed is a much worse trust violation, on an app whose entire pitch is "we don't lie to you about your own data." I'd rather ship a slightly conservative stuck-check than an exact one we don't have time to prove correct.

Last thing, since I promised concrete acceptance criteria and mostly gestured at the idea last round instead of writing them: the Stats screen needs an explicit empty state before any game exists for that mode, and that's not optional polish — it's the global "every screen needs empty/loading/success/error" rule colliding directly with the "N/A best time" and "no fabricated data" rules we've already locked. Acceptance criteria should read something like: on first launch, before any game is completed in a given draw mode, that mode's stats show a real empty state ("0 games played" or equivalent), never a placeholder number, never the other mode's numbers, and never blank. And for the draw-mode setting specifically: selecting draw-3 while a draw-1 game is mid-progress must trigger the same confirmation pattern already locked for New Game — if the player confirms, the current game is discarded and a fresh draw-3 deal starts; if they cancel, the setting value doesn't change and the in-progress game is untouched. That's the kind of criterion that's actually testable by someone poking at the app, not just prose we hope gets implemented faithfully.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift

    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

The product should be a fast, trustworthy Klondike session that always feels like a real table game first and an app shell second, so I’d build the UX around one core promise: instant playability and honest state, then premium motion and visual identity as a confirming layer.  
The design language is “Velvet Tabletop Atelier”: soft radial-vellum gradients under matte card stock textures, embossed suit glyphs with strict typographic hierarchy, and restrained contrast bands for both light and dark mode so the game reads like a real, expensive physical object even when a hand is incomplete. The rationale is that this app succeeds only if it visibly rejects the “tutorial-card” look while still letting players identify cards and plan moves in under a second.  
The emotional target is: open app, glance at the tableau, and immediately trust the board is live, legible, and yours to solve.

Signature interaction is the cold-launch-first-deal: per-card spring release from a depth stack, then a timed flip-deal cadence into tableau columns with a soft settling settle, where each card lands with micro-parallax shadows that imply weight and table friction. If that motion is clean on launch and legal moves feel equally tactile, it becomes the identity of the app.  
I would reject the default stock iOS solitaire look on three concrete points: first, replace plain rounded-rect cards with custom bespoke faces, backs, and paper grain from one generative grammar; second, swap the flat gray/blue grid into a textured felt+laminated table field with semantic depth layers so every pile has visual affordance before interaction; third, replace generic UIKit card rows with custom hit-target aware stack views that can express destination highlights without turning a face-down pile into a random icon grid, and avoid default chrome like plain lists and system forms in all key screens.

Screen inventory for this phase is fixed at three peers in TabView: Game, Stats, Settings, with the app launching directly to Game and restoring saved state if present.  
The Game screen has an active layout state: active in-progress game (deal/flip already done), selecting source card state (candidate run computed), destination-choice highlight state for multi-destination taps, blocked-move feedback state, win terminal, and stuck-terminal.  
The same screen also has small utility states that are visible and recoverable: empty-save recovery when decode fails, invalid-saved-state error with reset fallback, and pending confirmation state for New Game or in-progress draw-mode switch; no hidden transitions, no silent resets.  
Stats has three explicit states per mode: never-played empty state per draw mode with explanatory icon+copy+action, populated success state with games won/played/best time/streak, and local persistence error state if the stats file cannot be parsed (with reset/rebuild option, never fake numbers).  
Settings has live states for Card Back selection, Draw mode, and Timer toggle with immediate, local persistence confirmation, plus disclosure-copy state about device-local persistence and an explicit “restart required” confirmation path for draw-mode changes while a game is in progress.  

Primary user flow starts in Game: launch resolves active state, user sees tableau immediately, taps a source card, app highlights legal destinations or runs auto-accept with haptics and spring motion, or indicates blocked move if none. Every legal move is one tap-to-move flow; run moves happen as a whole run unit while live drag remains out of scope. Stock draw updates table state and timer if it has not started. Undo is always available in-game as an inline action and returns exact state. On terminal condition (win or stuck) the game shows a full-state action sheet with New Game and return-to-game context; New Game always asks if current game is unfinished. Stats and Settings are always reachable via tabs, and Settings draw-mode change while active game follows the same confirmation component as New Game.

State model should be explicit and deterministic: for Game, persisted logical state is {deck pools, face-up flags, active draw mode, timer status/start offset, move history pointer, terminal flags}. For Stats, state is {per-mode totals: games played, won, best time optional, streak, N/A marker}. For Settings, state is {draw mode, card back id, timer enabled, disclosure acknowledged}; all changes are local and immediate except draw-mode, which is confirmation-gated. In the UI layer, each of these has success, loading, and error surfaces even though there is no backend; loading is relevant during startup restoration and settings persistence writes, error only appears for decode/persistence recovery.

Accessibility is not optional on this custom-card stack, so every card must expose explicit labels (“Seven of Hearts, tableau column three, face up” style), directional order in VoiceOver, and non-color-only suit/sequence cues. Motion must respect reduced-motion by using gentler fade/translate in place of full spring/deal arcs where needed, and legal/illegal move feedback should be perceivable through haptics plus non-visual state.  

The smallest risky but highest-value cut is this: keep draw-1 and draw-3, two draw modes in one coherent engine, plus immediate TabView triad (Game/Stats/Settings), but hold off adding alternate interaction surfaces that dilute the rules pipeline; everything else should be built as part of correctness and state honesty first. The biggest objection I would raise against this direction is visual ambition can still outrun card-legibility at true on-device width, so the design spec must preserve a hard legibility gate as a release gate, not a design review note, and the final build must keep the 45–50pt card width playable and unambiguous.
